lessons.title: Hotel KPIs: occupancy, ADR and RevPAR
lessons.summary: The three numbers every hotel revenue meeting starts with.

steps.title: Volume, price and both together
steps.body:
Occupancy = rooms sold / available rooms (how full).
ADR (average daily rate) = room revenue / rooms sold (the average price of a sold room).
RevPAR (revenue per available room) = room revenue / available rooms (how well the hotel monetises its whole capacity).

When the periods and room counts match: RevPAR = ADR × Occupancy (occupancy as a decimal).
steps.deeper: Available rooms means available room nights for the period: rooms × days. If no rooms were sold, ADR is undefined (not $0); if no rooms were available, occupancy and RevPAR are undefined. FinPilot shows these as n/a. RevPAR counts room revenue only; TRevPAR (total revenue per available room) adds F&B and other revenue. None of these are profit measures: a high RevPAR can still come with high distribution costs.

steps.title: Harbour Crest, one January (fictional)
steps.note: RevPAR is always at or below ADR, because occupancy cannot exceed 100%.

steps.title: Calculate RevPAR
steps.prompt: In B5, calculate RevPAR from the data above it.
hints: RevPAR divides room revenue by available rooms, not rooms sold.

steps.question: ADR is $300 and occupancy 70%. A 10% discount lifts occupancy to 75%. What happens to RevPAR?
steps.reveal: Before: $300 × 70% = $210. After: $270 × 75% = $202.50. More rooms sold, less revenue per available room.

steps.title: Rate versus occupancy
steps.prompt: Find combinations of ADR and occupancy that give the same RevPAR.
steps.observe: $300 at 70% and $262.50 at 80% both give RevPAR of $210, but the second sells 540 more rooms, which means more cleaning, laundry and commissions.

steps.title: Why RevPAR and not occupancy alone
steps.body: Occupancy rewards filling rooms at any price; ADR rewards high prices even with empty rooms. RevPAR combines both into revenue earned per room the hotel could have sold.
steps.misconception: Higher occupancy is not automatically better. Selling more rooms at lower rates can lower RevPAR and raises variable costs, so profit can fall.

steps.title: Monthly KPI pack
steps.scenario: Harbour Crest (180 rooms) sold 4,185 room nights in a 31-day month for room revenue of $1,422,900.
steps.question: What was RevPAR?

mistakes.message: $340 is ADR (revenue per room sold). RevPAR divides by available rooms: 180 × 31 = 5,580.
You divided by the number of rooms only. Use room nights: rooms × days.

questions.question: Room revenue $1,650,000 from 4,400 rooms sold. ADR?
A hotel closed for renovation sold zero rooms in a month. What should the model show for ADR?
questions.explanation: ADR divides by rooms sold. With zero rooms sold it is undefined; showing $0 would suggest rooms were given away.

points: RevPAR = room revenue / available = ADR × occupancy.
Undefined ratios are n/a, never zero.

lessons.title: Revenue drivers: price, volume and mix
lessons.summary: Build total revenue from rooms, F&B and other departments.

steps.title: Revenue = drivers multiplied together
steps.body:
A driver-based forecast builds revenue from operational assumptions rather than guessing a total:
• Rooms sold = available room nights × occupancy
• Room revenue = rooms sold × ADR
• F&B revenue = rooms sold × F&B spend per occupied room
• Other revenue = room revenue × other-revenue %
• Total operating revenue = the sum of all streams.
steps.deeper: These are simplifications. Real hotels forecast F&B with covers × average check per outlet, banqueting by event, and segment-level room revenue (leisure, corporate, group) each with its own volume and rate. That segment detail creates mix effects: the blended ADR changes when the share of each segment changes, even if no individual rate changes.

steps.title: One month of drivers (fictional)
steps.note: Change occupancy and all three streams move.

steps.title: Total operating revenue
steps.prompt: In B5, calculate total operating revenue: room revenue + F&B revenue + other revenue, from the drivers in B1:B4.
hints: F&B = B1*B3; other = room revenue × B4.

steps.question: Occupancy rises while ADR and spend per room are unchanged. What happens to F&B revenue in this model?
options: Rises in proportion to rooms sold
steps.reveal: F&B is driven by occupied rooms, so it moves with rooms sold.

steps.title: Drive the revenue
steps.observe: A rate rise lifts room and other revenue; an occupancy rise lifts all three streams.

steps.title: Drivers explain the 'why'
steps.body: Because every line traces back to occupancy, rate or spend, a driver model explains variances: you can say revenue missed budget because occupancy was 3 points lower, not just that it missed.
steps.misconception: Room revenue is not total revenue, and neither is profit. Keep revenue streams separate so their different margins can be modelled later.

steps.title: Blended ADR
steps.scenario: In one month Harbour Crest sold 2,000 leisure room nights at $380, 1,200 corporate at $290 and 800 group at $230.
steps.question: What is the blended ADR across all segments?

mistakes.message: $300 is the simple average of the three rates. ADR must be weighted by rooms sold: total revenue / total rooms.

hints: Total room revenue / total rooms sold.

questions.question: If the share of lower-rated group business rises while every segment's rate is unchanged, blended ADR:
Which is a driver rather than a result?
questions.explanation: Spend per room is an assumption that drives F&B revenue.

points: Build revenue from drivers: volume × price.
Separate room, F&B and other revenue.
Blended ADR is revenue-weighted; mix changes it.
formulas: F&B revenue = Rooms sold × Spend per occupied room

lessons.title: Seasonality and weighted results
lessons.summary: Monthly patterns, seasonal indices and why you never average percentages.

steps.title: Demand has a calendar
steps.body:
Hotels have predictable seasonal patterns: Harbour Crest is busiest in July-August and quietest in January-February. A seasonal index describes each month relative to the average month (1.18 = 18% above average).

Annual or quarterly KPIs must be weighted: annual occupancy = total rooms sold / total available, not the average of twelve monthly percentages.
steps.deeper: Seasonality is estimated from history (several years of monthly data) and adjusted for known events. Applying an index can push a month above 100% occupancy; a model must cap it and recognise that demand above capacity is lost (or shifts to rate). Trends (year-on-year growth) sit on top of seasonality.

steps.title: Two months, one wrong shortcut
steps.body: January: 31 days at 50% occupancy. February: 28 days at 90%. 100 rooms.
steps.note: The average overweights the shorter month.

steps.title: Weighted occupancy
steps.prompt: In B5, calculate occupancy for January-April from available room nights (row 2) and rooms sold (row 3). Do not average the monthly percentages.
hints: Weighted occupancy = total sold / total available.

steps.question: January (31 days) runs at 50% and February (28 days) at 90%. Combined occupancy is:
steps.reveal: January has more nights, so its lower rate carries more weight: 69.0%.

steps.title: Seasonal index
steps.prompt: Apply indices to an average occupancy and watch for months that exceed capacity.
steps.observe: Push the average to 90% with a 1.18 index: unconstrained demand is 106%, so the model caps at 100% and that demand is lost. That is the case for raising rates in peak months.

steps.title: Weighting and capacity
steps.body: Weighted totals respect month length and volume. Capacity caps remind you that demand above 100% is lost unless price rises.
steps.misconception: Averaging ratios (occupancy, ADR, margins) across periods is one of the most common modeling mistakes. Recompute ratios from totals.

steps.title: Phase a target
steps.scenario: The annual occupancy target is 78% and July's seasonal index is 1.18.
steps.question: What occupancy should July be budgeted at (before any cap)?

mistakes.message: You added 18 percentage points. An index of 1.18 multiplies: 78% × 1.18.

questions.question: Annual ADR should be calculated as:
options: Total room revenue / total rooms sold
questions.explanation: Recompute from totals so busy months carry their proper weight.

questions.question: A seasonal index of 0.85 for November means:
options: November is 15% below the average month
questions.explanation: Indices are relative to the average month.

points: Seasonal indices describe each month relative to average.
Cap occupancy at 100%; excess demand is lost.
Weighted (from totals), never averaged, for multi-period ratios.

lessons.title: Actual, budget, forecast and variance
lessons.summary: Compare plans with reality and label variances correctly.

steps.title: Three versions of the numbers
steps.body:
Budget: the approved plan, set before the year, usually fixed. Forecast: the latest best estimate, updated during the year. Actual: what really happened.

Variance = actual (or forecast) - budget. For revenue, positive is favourable; for costs, positive is unfavourable.
steps.deeper: Variance % = variance / budget. Report variances in amounts and percentages, explain the driver behind each material variance (volume, rate, mix, cost per unit), and say what action follows. A 'material' threshold (e.g. ±5% or ±$50,000) focuses commentary on what matters.

steps.title: Harbour Crest January room revenue (fictional)
steps.note: A competitor's opening reduced winter demand.

steps.title: Variance percentage
steps.prompt: In B4, calculate the variance of actual (B1) against budget (B2) as a percentage of budget.

steps.question: Payroll cost was $520,000 against a budget of $480,000. The variance is:
steps.reveal: Actual minus budget is +$40,000. For a cost, spending more than budget is unfavourable.

steps.title: Label the variance
steps.prompt: Change actual and budget and see how the label depends on the line type.

outputs.label: If this is a REVENUE line
If this is a COST line

steps.observe: The same +$40,000 is favourable for revenue and unfavourable for cost.

steps.title: Sign conventions avoid confusion
steps.body: Keep one consistent rule (actual - budget) and add a favourable/unfavourable label. Readers then never have to guess what a minus sign means.
steps.misconception: A forecast is not a budget revision. The budget stays fixed for accountability; the forecast changes as information arrives.

steps.title: January variance
steps.scenario: Budget for January assumed 180 rooms × 31 nights × 62% occupancy × $285 ADR. Actual room revenue was $896,760.
steps.question: What is the variance against budget as a percentage? (Use a minus sign if below budget.)

mistakes.message: Right size, wrong sign: actual is below budget, so the variance is negative (unfavourable).
You divided by actual. Variance % is measured against budget.

questions.question: Which is updated during the year?
questions.explanation: Forecasts are revised; the budget stays as the fixed reference.

questions.question: Energy costs were $8,000 below budget. This variance is:
questions.explanation: Spending less than budget on a cost is favourable (though check it is not a timing difference).

points: Budget = plan; forecast = latest estimate; actual = reality.
Variance = actual - budget; label it favourable/unfavourable by line type.
Explain material variances by driver and action.

lessons.title: Revenue bridges: volume and rate
lessons.summary: Split a room revenue variance into what came from rooms sold and what came from price.

steps.title: Two levers, one variance
steps.body:
Room revenue = rooms sold × ADR, so a variance has two sources:
• Volume effect = (actual rooms - budget rooms) × budget ADR
• Rate effect = (actual ADR - budget ADR) × actual rooms
The two add up exactly to the total variance. A chart of these steps is a revenue bridge (or waterfall).
steps.deeper: The order matters: here volume is valued at budget rate and rate at actual volume, so there is no unexplained residual. Some companies use a third 'mix' or 'joint' effect; whatever method you use, document it and make sure the bridge reconciles to the total. Never insert an unexplained 'other' bar to force it to tie.

steps.title: Bridging January (fictional)
steps.body: Budget: 3,459.6 rooms at $285. Actual: 3,180 rooms at $282.
steps.note: Most of the miss came from volume, not price.

steps.title: Rate effect
steps.prompt: In B6, calculate the rate effect: (actual ADR - budget ADR) × actual rooms sold.
hints: Price difference × the rooms actually sold.

steps.question: Rooms sold are 5% above budget and ADR is 5% below budget. Room revenue versus budget is:
steps.reveal: 1.05 × 0.95 = 0.9975: 0.25% below budget. The effects do not cancel exactly.

steps.title: Build the bridge
steps.prompt: Change the four drivers and check that the bridge always reconciles.
steps.observe: Raise ADR while cutting rooms: the effects take opposite signs but still sum to the total.

steps.title: From numbers to story
steps.body: A bridge turns 'we missed by $89k' into 'we sold 280 fewer rooms (-$80k) at a slightly lower rate (-$10k)'. That points to the action: demand generation, not pricing.
steps.misconception: Bridges must reconcile. If the bars do not add to the total, a formula is wrong; do not add a balancing bar.

steps.title: Volume effect
steps.scenario: Budget: 180 rooms × 31 nights × 62% occupancy at $285 ADR. Actual: 3,180 rooms sold.
steps.question: What is the volume effect? (Negative if fewer rooms were sold.)

mistakes.message: You valued the volume difference at the actual ADR ($282). In this method volume is valued at budget ADR.

questions.question: Why is volume valued at budget ADR in this bridge?
options: So that volume and rate effects add up exactly to the total variance
questions.explanation: Budget-rate volume plus actual-volume rate effect reconciles with no residual.

questions.question: Budget 4,000 rooms at $300. Actual 4,200 rooms at $290. Rate effect?

mistakes.message: Rate effect uses actual rooms (4,200), not budget rooms.

points: Volume at budget rate; rate at actual volume.
A bridge must reconcile to the total.
formulas: Volume effect = (Actual rooms - Budget rooms) × Budget ADR
Rate effect = (Actual ADR - Budget ADR) × Actual rooms

lessons.title: Sensitivity and forecast limits
lessons.summary: Which assumptions matter most, and how wrong forecasts can be.

steps.title: What if we are wrong?
steps.body:
Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time and measures the effect on an output. A scenario changes several assumptions together to tell a coherent story (budget, downside, upside).

Forecast accuracy is measured after the fact, e.g. absolute percentage error = |actual - forecast| / actual.
steps.deeper: Forecasts are estimates, not facts. Limitations: history may not repeat (new competitors, events), drivers interact (higher rates can reduce occupancy), and small errors compound across months. Good practice: show ranges, name the key assumptions, track accuracy over time (mean absolute percentage error, MAPE) and say what would change your view.

steps.title: Two-way sensitivity (fictional annual room revenue)
steps.body: Harbour Crest forecast: $17.48m. Rows: occupancy shift; columns: ADR shift.
steps.note: Open the Hotel Simulation Center to recalculate this table live.

steps.title: Forecast error
steps.prompt: In B3, calculate the absolute percentage error of the forecast (B2) against the actual (B1).
hints: Error size regardless of direction: ABS().

steps.question: Occupancy is 75% and ADR $300. Which raises RevPAR more: +5 occupancy points or +5% ADR?
steps.reveal: +5 points is +6.7% relative (80/75); +5% ADR is +5%. Percentage points and percent are different sizes of change.

steps.title: Shock the assumptions
steps.prompt: Apply shifts to occupancy (points) and ADR (%).
steps.observe: -10 points of occupancy costs 13.3% of RevPAR; a 10% rate cut costs 10%.

steps.title: Know your big levers
steps.body: Sensitivity shows where to focus research and management attention. It also protects decision-makers from false precision: a single-point forecast hides the range of plausible outcomes.
steps.misconception: A forecast is not a promise. Present it with its assumptions, a range and its track record.

steps.title: Mean absolute percentage error
steps.scenario: Three months: actual $1,000,000 vs forecast $960,000; actual $1,200,000 vs forecast $1,272,000; actual $900,000 vs forecast $918,000.
steps.question: What is the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE)?

mistakes.message: You averaged signed errors, so over- and under-forecasts cancelled. MAPE uses absolute values.
Signed errors cancelled before you took the absolute value. Take the absolute value of each month first.

questions.question: A downside scenario differs from a sensitivity because it:
options: Changes one input at a time
Changes several related assumptions together to tell a coherent story
questions.explanation: Scenarios combine consistent assumptions; sensitivities isolate one.

questions.question: Which statement about a forecast is correct?
options: It is an estimate based on stated assumptions and should be shown with its key risks

points: Sensitivity: one input at a time; scenario: a consistent set.
Percentage-point and percent shifts differ in size.
Measure accuracy (MAPE) and present ranges, not guarantees.
